title: Robotic radical prostatectomy
subtitle: Bladder neck, seminal vesicles, nerves, apex, then a watertight anastomosis

sources.title: NG131 Prostate cancer: diagnosis and management
BAUS procedure-specific patient information and consent guidance

indications: Localised (or selected locally advanced) prostate cancer with a life expectancy that makes cure worthwhile, chosen after MDT and discussion of radiotherapy and surveillance.
contraindications: Unfit for steep Trendelenburg and pneumoperitoneum.
preparation: MRI, PSMA PET or bone scan per risk; MDT decision and nerve-sparing plan per side.
Consent: incontinence, erectile dysfunction, positive margin and further treatment, rectal injury, lymphocele.
positioning: Lithotomy with steep Trendelenburg (about 25 to 30 degrees), arms tucked and padded, the patient secured against sliding, eyes protected.
equipment: Robot, bipolar and monopolar instruments, clips, barbed suture for the anastomosis, catheter, retrieval bag.
anatomy: Bladder neck, seminal vesicles and vasa, Denonvilliers' fascia, neurovascular bundles, dorsal venous complex, urethra and sphincter, rectum.
criticalSafety: Preserve the neurovascular bundles where cancer allows.
Avoid the rectum behind Denonvilliers' fascia; test if in doubt.
commonErrors: Cutting into the prostate at the apex (positive margin).
postop: Catheter for about 7 to 10 days; pelvic floor exercises.

steps.emphasis: Continence, erections, margins and further treatment discussed.
Staging, nerve-sparing plan per side and node dissection decision confirmed.
Lithotomy with steep Trendelenburg, arms tucked and padded, secured against sliding, eyes protected.
Extended pelvic node dissection when indicated: external iliac, obturator and internal iliac, protecting the obturator nerve.
Fill with about 150 ml and check the anastomosis.
Prostate in a bag, out intact.
Catheter for about 7 to 10 days; it must not be removed early.

step.rp.bladder-drop.title: Drop the bladder into the space of Retzius
step.rp.bladder-drop.why: Opening the space in front of the bladder exposes the front of the prostate and the endopelvic fascia.
how: Incise the peritoneum lateral to the medial umbilical ligaments and across above the bladder.
Develop the avascular space of Retzius down to the pubic bone.
Clear fat off the front of the prostate.

step.rp.bladder-neck.title: Bladder neck dissection
step.rp.bladder-neck.why: Finding the junction of bladder and prostate right preserves the bladder neck and keeps away from the ureteric orifices.
how: Find the junction by moving the catheter balloon and the change in fat.
Open the anterior bladder neck, lift the catheter, then divide the posterior bladder neck.
Check the ureteric orifices are well away from the cut edge.
pitfalls: Cutting into the prostate (positive margin) or too far into the bladder.

step.rp.seminal-vesicles.title: Seminal vesicles and posterior plane
step.rp.seminal-vesicles.why: The vasa and seminal vesicles lead to the plane behind the prostate, in front of the rectum.
how: Divide the vasa and dissect the seminal vesicles, clipping their arteries rather than burning near the nerves.
Lift the seminal vesicles and incise Denonvilliers' fascia.
Develop the plane between the prostate and the rectum towards the apex.
pitfalls: Thermal energy at the tip of the seminal vesicles near the nerves.

step.rp.nerves.title: Pedicles and nerve sparing
step.rp.nerves.why: The neurovascular bundles run beside the prostate. Releasing them without heat gives the best chance of erections.
how: Control the prostatic pedicles with clips close to the prostate, without diathermy.
Release the neurovascular bundle off the prostate in the planned plane (intrafascial or interfascial) on each side.
Do not spare a nerve on a side with high-risk cancer.

step.rp.apex.title: Dorsal venous complex and apex
step.rp.apex.why: The apex is where positive margins and incontinence are decided. A long urethral stump with clean margins is the goal.
how: Control the dorsal venous complex with a suture.
Divide it and develop the apex, then cut the urethra sharply with cold scissors, keeping its length.
Check the apex of the specimen for capsule.

step.rp.rectal-injury.title: Bailout: rectal injury
step.rp.rectal-injury.why: A rectal injury recognised now and repaired heals; one missed becomes a rectourethral fistula.
how: If suspected, fill the pelvis with saline and insufflate air via the rectum; look for bubbles.
Repair in two layers, interpose tissue where possible, and wash out.
Call a colorectal surgeon if needed; consider a defunctioning stoma for a large or contaminated injury; record it.
pitfalls: Not testing after a difficult posterior dissection.

step.rp.anastomosis.title: Vesicourethral anastomosis
step.rp.anastomosis.why: A watertight, tension-free join of the bladder neck to the urethra lets the catheter come out on time and lowers stricture risk.
how: Optionally reconstruct the posterior layer (Rocco) to reduce tension.
Join bladder neck to urethra with a running barbed or double-armed suture, mucosa to mucosa.
Pass a new catheter under vision before completing the front.
pitfalls: Catching the catheter in the stitch.
Bites that take the ureteric orifice.
